definition: Forsake, leave behind.
example: We abandoned the old car in the empty parking lot.
etymology: Compare typologically abdicate, Russian отказа́ться (otkazátʹsja) (akin to приказа́ть (prikazátʹ), сказа́ть (skazátʹ), указа́ть (ukazátʹ)).

definition: Forsaken by owner or inhabitants.
example: Weed-grown yard of an abandoned farmhouse.
etymology: From Middle English abandoned, equivalent to abandon + -ed.

definition: A child who has been abandoned and whose parents are unknown.
A church associated with a monastery or convent.
example: From 1199 to 1203 William Punchard was the abbot of the abbey of Rievaulx, which was part of the Cistercian order of monks.

definition: Mentioned or named earlier in the same text.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:above-mentioned.

definition: Not being in a specified place.
example: When they were able to return to the clinic some months later, certain pieces of equipment were absent.
etymology: From Middle English absent, from Middle French absent, from Old French ausent, and their source, Latin absens, present participle of absum (“to be away from”), from ab (“away”) + sum (“to be”).

definition: The maximum altitude at which an airplane can maintain horizontal flight.
(astronomy) the magnitude that a star would have if it were viewed from a distance of 10 parsecs (32.62 light years) from the earth.

Instrumental music, as a concerto or string quartet, that draws no inspiration from or makes no reference to a text, program, visual image, or title and that exists solely in terms of its musical form, structure, and elements.
Physical space independent of what occupies it.
The lowest level of stimulation that a person can detect.
A real number regardless of its sign.
example: The absolute value |x| of a real number x is √x², which is equal to x if x is non-negative, and -x if x is negative.

definition: Become imbued.
example: The liquids, light, and gases absorb.
etymology: From Middle French absorber, from Old French assorbir, from Latin absorbeō (“swallow up”), from ab- (“from”) + sorbeō (“suck in, swallow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ- (“to sip”). Compare French absorber.

definition: Giving or marked by complete attention to.
example: Fully absorbed.
etymology: From absorb + -ed.

definition: A painter of abstract pictures.
A general concept formed by extracting common features from specific examples.
Inconsistent with reason or logic or common sense.
example: The absurd predicament of seeming to argue that virtue is highly desirable but intensely unpleasant.
etymology: First attested in 1557. From Middle French absurde, from Latin absurdus (“incongruous, dissonant, out of tune”), from ab (“away from, out”) + surdus (“silent, deaf, dull-sounding”). Compare surd.

definition: The property of a more than adequate quantity or supply.
example: An age of abundance.
etymology: From Middle English abundaunce, habaundance, from Old French habundance, abondance, from Latin abundantia (“fullness, plenty”), from abundō (“to overflow”). Equivalent to abound + -ance.

definition: Used improperly or excessively especially drugs.
example: An abused substance.

definition: An administrator in a college or university.
A style of painting and sculpture produced under the influence of European academies of art.
A costume worn on formal occasions by the faculty or students of a university or college.
An award conferred by a college or university signifying that the recipient has satisfactorily completed a course of study.
(education) a program of education in liberal arts and sciences (usually in preparation for higher education).
A requirement for admission to or completion of an academic program.
The time during which a school holds classes.
The period of time each year when the school is open and people are studying.
example: In many countries the academic year starts in September and finishes in August of the next calendar year.

definition: A diacritical mark used to indicate stress or placed above a vowel to indicate a special pronunciation.
example: The name of the French painter Paul Cézanne is written with an acute accent mark.

definition: Having more than the average number of accidents.
Happening by chance or unexpectedly or unintentionally.
example: Accidental poisoning.
etymology: From Middle English accidental, from Anglo-Norman accidentel, Middle French accidentel, accidental, and their source, Late Latin accidēntālis; corresponding to accident + -al.

definition: Be agreeable or acceptable to.
etymology: First use appears c.

definition: Making or becoming suitable; adjusting to circumstances.
example: I have booked the accommodation for my trip to Paris.
etymology: From French accommodation, from Latin accommodātiō (“adjustment, accommodation, compliance”), from accommodō (“adapt, put in order”). Superficially accommodate + -ion. The sense of "lodging" was first attested in 1600.

definition: Be present or associated with an event or entity.
example: Heart attacks are accompanied by destruction of heart tissue.
etymology: From Middle English accompanien, from Old French acompagner (“to associate with”), from compaing (“companion”), nominative singular of compaignon (“companion”). See company.

definition: Occurring with or following as a consequence.
Put in effect.
example: To accomplish a design, an object, a promise.

definition: Harmony of people's opinions or actions or characters.
example: The accord of light and shade in painting.
etymology: From Middle English accord, from Old French acort, from acorder (see verb below).

definition: (sentence connectors) because of the reason given.
example: Continued to have severe headaches and accordingly returned to the doctor.
etymology: From Middle English acordingli, equivalent to according + -ly.

definition: Someone in charge of a client's account for an advertising agency or brokerage or other service business.
Responsibility to someone or for some activity.
etymology: From accountable + -ity.

definition: Liable to account for one's actions.
example: Governments must be accountable to someone beside themselves.
etymology: From account + -able. First attested around 1400.

definition: A principle that governs current accounting practice and that is used as a reference to determine the appropriate treatment of complex transactions.
A relative magnitude of two selected numerical values taken from an enterprise's financial statements.
Conforming exactly or almost exactly to fact or to a standard or performing with total accuracy.
example: An accurate reproduction.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin accūrātus, perfect passive participle of accūrō (“to take care of”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + cūrō (“care for”). First attested in 1610. Compare English cure.

definition: With few mistakes.
example: He works very accurately.
etymology: From accurate + -ly.

definition: Someone who takes LSD.
A hydrogen atom in an acid that forms a positive ion when the acid dissociates.
Yielding an acid in aqueous solution.
etymology: From acid + forming.

definition: Recognized or made known or admitted.
example: The acknowledged leader of the community.

definition: A device for amplifying or transmitting sound.
Sound is not amplified by electrical means.
example: He was playing the acoustic guitar while his girlfriend was on the drums.
etymology: Retronym for guitar, coined after the invention of the electric guitar to refer to the older type of guitar and avoid confusion with the electric guitar.

definition: The physical intensity of sound.
Opposition to the flow of sound through a surface; acoustic resistance is the real component of acoustic impedance and acoustic reactance is the imaginary component.
The distribution of energy as a function of frequency for a particular sound source.
A storage device consisting of acoustic delay lines.
(acoustics) a wave that transmits sound.
The act of acquiring something.
example: I envied his talent for acquiring.

definition: One twelfth of an acre-foot.
The volume of water that would cover 1 acre to a depth of 1 foot; 43,560 cubic feet or 1233.5 cubic meters.
Act like the master of.
A New York school of painting characterized by freely created abstractions; the first important school of American painting to develop independently of European styles.
The immediate rebroadcast of some action (especially sports action) that has been recorded on videotape.
(of sewage) treated with aeration and bacteria to aid decomposition.
Powdered or granular carbon used for purifying by adsorption; given orally (as a slurry) it is an antidote for some kinds of poisons.
Stimulation of activity in an organism or chemical.
example: Using shopper activation to convert shoppers into buyers.
etymology: From active + -ation, or from activate + -ion.

definition: The energy that an atomic system must acquire before a process (such as an emission or reaction) can occur.
example: Catalysts are said to reduce the energy of activation during the transition phase of a reaction.

definition: Chemical agent capable of activity.
An application that is currently running and in the foreground.
Childbirth during which the mother is encouraged to be an active participant.
Money, or property that may readily be converted into money.
A form of acquired immunity in which the body produces its own antibodies against disease-causing antigens.
The voice used to indicate that the grammatical subject of the verb is performing the action or causing the happening denoted by the verb.
example: ‘The boy threw the ball’ uses the active voice.

definition: (law) compensation for losses that can readily be proven to have occurred and for which the injured party has the right to be compensated.
An angle less than 90 degrees but more than 0 degrees.
An agency that designs advertisement to call public attention to its clients.
An organized program of advertisements.
For an intervening time; temporarily.
example: Elected to serve ad interim.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ad interim (“in the meantime”).

definition: Make fit for, or change to suit a new purpose.
example: Adapt our native cuisine to the available food resources of the new country.
etymology: From Middle English *adapten (attested in Middle English adapted (past participle)), from Latin adaptāre (“to fit to”), from ad- (“to”) + aptāre (“to make fit”), from aptus (“fit”); see apt.

definition: Compulsively or physiologically dependent on something habit-forming.
example: She is addicted to chocolate.

definition: A formal exploration of addictions from a variety of academic and scientific perspectives: sociological, cultural, psychological, anthropological, and psychoanalytic.
A calculator that performs simple arithmetic functions.
A chemical reaction in which one molecule is added to another.
A printer that automatically prints addresses on letters for mailing.
Having the requisite qualities or resources to meet a task.
example: She had adequate training.

definition: Having the requisite qualities for.
Alter or regulate so as to achieve accuracy or conform to a standard.
example: Adjust the clock, please.

definition: Making or becoming suitable; adjusting to circumstances.
A price dictated by any entity other than market forces.
Of or relating to or responsible for administration.
A unit with administrative responsibilities.
The body of rules and regulations and orders and decisions created by administrative agencies of government.
Someone who administers a business.
The supreme commander of a fleet; ranks above a vice admiral and below a fleet admiral.
Feel admiration for.
example: To admire a person of high moral worth.
etymology: From Middle English admyren, borrowed from Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror, from ad + mīror (“wonder at”).

definition: The fee charged for admission.
The fee charged for admission.
Lovable especially in a childlike or naive way.
example: A romantic love song with adorable-sounding drum beats.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French adorable and its etymon Latin adōrābilis, from adōrāre + -bilis, from ad + ōrō. By surface analysis, adore + -able.

definition: A course (via lectures or correspondence) for adults who are not otherwise engaged in formal study.
An adult female person (as opposed to a man).
The average IQ of the adults in a given population.
An adult person who is male (as opposed to a woman).
Any of the 32 teeth that replace the deciduous teeth of early childhood and (with luck) can last until old age.
Encouragement of the progress or growth or acceptance of something.
example: The advancement of learning.
etymology: From Middle English avancement, Old French avancement. See advance. Morphologically advance + -ment.

definition: Moving forward.
Take a risk in the hope of a favorable outcome.
etymology: Compare Scots adventur, Swedish äventyr, German Abenteuer.

definition: A story of an adventure.
Contrary to your interests or welfare.
example: Adverse circumstances.

definition: An opinion concerning financial statements (usually based on an audit by a CPA) that the statements as a whole do not present results fairly or are not in conformity with the generally accepted accounting practices of the United States.
A situation where sellers have information that buyers don't (or vice versa) about some aspect of product quality.
example: The large number of "lemons" in the used-car market is the result of adverse selection.

definition: A witness whose relationship to the opposing party is such that his or her testimony may be prejudiced against the opposing party.
A public promotion of some product or service.
example: Companies try to sell their products using advertisements in form of placards, television spots and print publications.
etymology: From Middle French advertissement (“statement calling attention”), compare French avertissement (“warning”). See advertise. Equivalent to advertise + -ment.

definition: A public promotion of some product or service.
etymology: From advertise + -ing.

definition: An organized program of advertisements.
Give advice to.
example: The dentist advised me to brush three times a day.
etymology: From Middle English avisen (“to perceive, consider, inform”), from Old French aviser, from avis, or from Late Latin advisō, from ad + visō. See also advice.

definition: An expert who gives advice.
example: An adviser helped students select their courses.
etymology: From advise + -er.

definition: An expert who gives advice.
example: An adviser helped students select their courses.
etymology: From advise + -or.

definition: Active support of an idea or cause etc.; especially the act of pleading or arguing for something.
etymology: From Middle English advocacie, advocacye, advocatye, from Middle French advocacie, advocatie, avocacie and Medieval Latin advocātia; equivalent to advocate + -cy.

definition: An interest group that tries to influence legislators or bureaucrats to act in their favor, typically through lobbying.
Existing or living or growing or operating in the air.
example: Aerial roots of a philodendron.
etymology: From Latin āeri(us) + -al, from Ancient Greek ἀέριος (aérios), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + -ιος (-ios). By surface analysis, aer- (“air”) + -ial.

definition: Relating to or dealing with the subject of aesthetics.
example: It works well enough, but the shabby exterior offends his aesthetic sensibilities.
etymology: Cognates include Proto-Germanic *awiz (“obvious”), Sanskrit आविस् (āvís, “manifestly, evidently”) and Latin audiō.

definition: The semantic role of an entity that is not the agent but is directly involved in or affected by the happening denoted by the verb in the clause.
Arousing affect.
example: The homecoming of the released hostages was an affecting scene.

definition: A positive feeling of liking.
example: He had trouble expressing the affection he felt.
etymology: From Middle English affection, affeccion, affeccioun, from Old French affection, from Latin affectiōnem, from affectiō; equivalent to affect + -ion.

definition: A subordinate or subsidiary associate; a person who is affiliated with another or with an organization.
example: Our local TV channel is an affiliate of NBC.
etymology: From Medieval Latin affīliātus, the passive past participle of Late Latin adfīliō, affīliō (“to adopt as son”), from ad- + fīlius + -ō. Equivalent to Latin affīliō + -ate. Compare French affilié (noun).

definition: Being joined in close association.
example: Affiliated clubs.

definition: A blanket knitted or crocheted in strips or squares; sometimes used as a shawl.
etymology: From Afghan.

definition: A fragrant lotion for a man's face after shaving.
The consequences of an event (especially a catastrophic event).
example: The aftermath of war.
etymology: From after- + math (“a mowing”).

definition: A light midafternoon meal of tea and sandwiches or cakes.
example: An Englishman would interrupt a war to have his afternoon tea.

definition: Happening at a time subsequent to a reference time.
example: It didn't happen until afterward.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English afterward, from Old English æfterweard; equivalent to after + -ward.

definition: Happening at a time subsequent to a reference time.
example: It didn't happen until afterward.
etymology: From Middle English afterwardes, from Old English æfteweard (“behind”) + -s (“(adverbial genitive)”). By surface analysis, after + -wards.

definition: A group of people having approximately the same age.
Regulation establishing the maximum age for doing something or holding some position.
example: The bar's age limit was 21, so we could not get in.

definition: The average age at which particular performances are expected to appear.
A bank named by a lending syndicate of several banks to protect their interests.
In macroeconomics, the total demand for final goods and services in the economy at a given time and price level.
example: Schools of economics agree that during a time of economic downturn, government should cut taxes to increase aggregate demand.

definition: Fruit consisting of many individual small fruits or drupes derived from separate ovaries within a common receptacle: e.g. blackberry, raspberry, pineapple.
A disposition to behave aggressively.
etymology: From Middle French aggression, from Latin aggressio, from aggressus, past participle of aggredior (“to approach, address, attack”). By surface analysis, ag- + -gress + -ion.

definition: Acquiring desirable qualities by being left undisturbed for some time.
etymology: By surface analysis, age + -ing.

definition: Constituted or contracted by stipulation or agreement.
Study of both chemistry and biochemistry which are important in agricultural production, the processing of raw products into foods and beverages, and in environmental monitoring and remediation.
(military) a station located near a combat area for giving first aid to the wounded.
A safety restraint in an automobile; the bag inflates on collision and prevents the driver or passenger from being thrown forward.
Absentminded dreaming while awake.
A filter that removes dust from the air that passes through it.
etymology: From air + cleaner.

definition: A system that keeps air cool and dry.
example: This car has air conditioning.
etymology: From air + conditioning.

definition: The crew of an aircraft.
The flow of air.
example: She adjusted the fan so that the airflow was directed right at her.

definition: A local region of low pressure or descending air that causes a plane to lose height suddenly.
A male steward on an airplane.
A designated route followed by airplanes in flying from one airport to another.
A chamber that provides access to space where air is under pressure.
Mail that is sent by air transport.
A person trained by the government in hijacking and terrorist tactics who (for security reasons) is a passenger aboard an airline flight.
A local region of low pressure or descending air that causes a plane to lose height suddenly.
Yam of tropical Africa and Asia cultivated for it large tubers.
A shaft for ventilation.
Motion sickness experienced while traveling by air (especially during turbulence).
Transportation by air.
Transportation by air.
A sound wave that is transmitted via air.
Made dry by contact with unheated air.
Full of air.
Transport (cargo) by air.
example: Because of their urgency the agent will air-freight the parts.

definition: A duct that admits air to be mixed with fuel.
A truncated cloth cone mounted on a mast; used (e.g., at airports) to show the direction of the wind.
Having no weak points.
The engine that powers an aircraft.
A noncommissioned officer in the British Royal Air Force.
Open to or abounding in fresh air.
A hose that carries air under pressure.
etymology: From air + line.

definition: A commercial enterprise that provides scheduled flights for passengers.
An aircraft that has a fixed wing and is powered by propellers or jets.
example: The flight was delayed due to trouble with the airplane.
etymology: From air + plane as an alteration of aeroplane.

definition: Landing an aircraft.
Someone who is licensed to operate an aircraft in flight.
A ticket good for a trip on an airplane.
A charge paid for the take-off, landing and parking of aircraft, and the use of passenger facilities.
A clock that wakes a sleeper at some preset time.
The chemical group -OH.
Characteristic of or containing alcohol.
example: Alcoholic drinks.

definition: Excessive use of alcohol and alcoholic drinks.
A liquor or brew containing alcohol as the active agent.
example: Alcohol (or drink) ruined him.

definition: Error resulting from the choice of the wrong algorithm or method for achieving the intended result.
Brought into agreement or cooperation on the side of a faction, party, or cause.
Extreme, thorough.
example: Why is he in such an all-fired hurry?
etymology: Probably a euphemistic form of hell-fired.

definition: Broad in scope or content.
example: We stayed at an all-inclusive resort while we were in Bermuda, and even the golfing was free.

definition: According to what has been alleged.
example: He was on trial for allegedly murdering his wife.
etymology: From alleged + -ly.

definition: A narrow street with walls on both sides.
example: The parking lot to my friend's apartment building is in the alley.
etymology: From Middle English aleye, from Anglo-Norman aleie, feminine of alé, past participle of aler (“to go”) (French aller). Doublet of allée.

definition: A homeless cat.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:alley cat.

definition: Related by common characteristics or ancestry.
example: Allied species.

definition: An amount allowed or granted (as during a given period).
example: Travel allowance.
etymology: From Middle English allouance, from Old French alouance. Morphologically allow + -ance.

definition: A reserve fund created by a charge against profits in order to provide for changes in the value of a company's assets.
Side by side.
example: Ahoy! Bring your boat alongside.
etymology: From along + side; compare alongsides.

definition: An alloy of brass and zinc; used mainly for cold working.
An alloy of copper and tin that can be worked.
The radiation of alpha particles during radioactive decay.
The normal brainwave in the electroencephalogram of a person who is awake but relaxed; occurs with a frequency of 8-12 hertz.
The table in Christian churches where communion is given.
Cause to change; make different; cause a transformation.
example: The advent of the automobile may have altered the growth pattern of the city.
etymology: From Old French alterer (French altérer), from Medieval Latin alterāre (“to make other”), from Latin alter (“the other”), from al- (seen in alius (“other”), alienus (“of another”), etc.; see alias, alien, etc.) + compar.

definition: Changed in form or character without becoming something else.
example: The altered policy promised success.

definition: A method of childbirth that avoids intrusive high-tech medicine in favor of more natural and homely settings.
Energy derived from sources that do not use up natural resources or harm the environment.
The practice of medicine without the use of drugs; may involve herbal medicines or self-awareness or biofeedback or acupuncture.
In place of, or as an alternative to.
example: Alternatively we could buy a used car.
etymology: From alternative + -ly.

definition: Elevation especially above sea level or above the earth's surface.
example: The altitude gave her a headache.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin altitūdō (“height”), from altus (“high”).

definition: To a complete degree or to the full or entire extent; Completely or entirely.
example: It was not altogether her fault.
etymology: From Middle English altogeder, altogedere, equivalent to al- (“all”) + together. Cognate with Scots awthegither (“altogether”), Middle High German alzegater (“altogether”), Dutch altegaar.

definition: A silvery ductile metallic element found primarily in bauxite.
etymology: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1812, after the earlier 1807 New Latin form alumium. By surface analysis, Latin alumen + -um

definition: Manufacturers of aluminum considered as a group.
Manufacturers of aluminum considered as a group.
Filled with the emotional impact of overwhelming surprise or shock.
example: An amazed audience gave the magician a standing ovation.

definition: A deep yellow color.
example: An amber light illuminated the room.
etymology: From Middle English ambre, aumbre, from Old French aumbre, ambre, from Arabic عَنْبَر (ʕanbar, “ambergris”), from Middle Persian 𐭠𐭭𐭡𐭫 (ʾnbl /⁠ambar⁠/, “ambergris”). Compare English lamber, ambergris.

definition: Of green tinged with amber.
A cherished desire.
example: His ambition is to own his own business.

definition: Having a strong desire for success or achievement.
A vehicle that takes people to and from hospitals.
etymology: Borrowed from French ambulance, which replaced hôpital ambulant (“moving hospital”) via the suffix -ance, from Latin ambulō (“to walk; to go about”).

definition: Area reserved for persons leading the responsive ‘amens’.
A chest to hold ammunition.
The basic unit of electric current adopted under the Systeme International d'Unites.
example: A typical household circuit carries 15 to 50 amps.

definition: A collection of anecdotes about a person or place.
etymology: Formed from the Latin suffix -ana; compare ism (from -ism), itis (from -itis), phobia (from -phobia).

definition: Someone who is skilled at analyzing data.
etymology: From French analyste.

definition: Consider in detail and subject to an analysis in order to discover essential features or meaning.
example: Analyze a sonnet by Shakespeare.

definition: Examined carefully and methodically; broken down for consideration of constituent parts.
example: The analyzed data indicated surprising trends.

definition: A mechanical device that prevents a vessel from moving.
etymology: From Middle English anchoren, ankeren, either from the noun or perhaps (via Old French ancrer) from a Medieval Latin verb ancorare, from the same Latin word ancora.

definition: The chain or rope that attaches an anchor to a vessel.
A light in the rigging of a ship that is riding at anchor.
A toroidal shape.
A history of the ancient world.
example: Who cares if he said those things at the beginning of the year? That's ancient history now.

definition: Sharks with broad flat bodies and winglike pectoral fins but that swim the way sharks do.
A stiff or threatening gait.
Communication between animals (of the same species).
A disease that typically does not affect human beings.
Any fat obtained from animals.
example: Animal fat is high in saturated fatty acids.

definition: Fiber derived from animals.
The pedal extremity of vertebrates other than human beings.
Taxonomic kingdom comprising all living or extinct animals.
The leg of an animal.
Material derived from animals.
The physical (or animal) side of a person as opposed to the spirit or intellect.
Any oil obtained from animal substances.
A product made from animal material.
The outer covering of an animal.
One who trains or exhibits animals.
Having life or vigor or spirit.
example: An animated and expressive face.

definition: A gliding joint between the distal ends of the tibia and fibula and the proximal end of the talus.
etymology: Compare with Sanskrit अङ्ग (aṅga, “limb”), अङ्गुरि (aṅguri, “finger”), Latin angulus. Compare haunch and Greek prefix ἀγκυλο- (ankulo-, “joint, crooked, bent”). Doublet of angulus and angle.

definition: A gliding joint between the distal ends of the tibia and fibula and the proximal end of the talus.
Coming only to the ankle or knee.
example: She went to the Common to walk Max, but soon found herself ankle-deep in mud.

definition: The date on which an event occurred in some previous year (or the celebration of it).
Aroused to impatience or anger.
example: Judy is annoyed at Jim because he forgot to put the bins out again.

definition: An annual formation of wood in plants as they grow.
Replying.
example: An answering glance.
etymology: From Middle English answerynge; equivalent to answer + -ing.

definition: An electronic device that answers the telephone and records messages.
Large shaggy-haired toothless anteater with long tongue and powerful claws; of South America.
A song of devotion or loyalty (as to a nation or school).
A situation where sellers have information that buyers don't (or vice versa) about some aspect of product quality.
Any form of drama which is not naturalistic, traditional, conventional or ‘legit’; thus, theatre which disobeys or actively goes against accepted laws and rules of dramaturgy.
example: Most anti-theatre, including Six Characters in Search of an Author, never achieves that level of acceptance in the mind of the audience.

definition: Expected hopefully.
A cover term for a variety of mental disorders in which severe anxiety is a salient symptom.
Used to indicate that a statement explains or supports a previous statement.
example: I don't know what happened to it; anyway, it's gone.
etymology: From any + adverbial genitive of way (compare always).

definition: A suite of rooms usually on one floor of an apartment house.
A building that is divided into apartments.
A building that is divided into apartments.
example: Heritage House is a ten-story apartment house for seniors in the heart of downtown.

definition: An expression of regret at having caused trouble for someone.
example: He wrote a letter of apology to the hostess.

definition: The line at which the sky and Earth appear to meet.
A board of officials that are not judicial but are appointed to hear appeals.
Able to attract interest or draw favorable attention.
example: He added an appealing and memorable figure to popular American mythology.
etymology: By surface analysis, appeal + -ing.

definition: Outward or visible aspect of a person or thing.
A feeling of craving something.
example: An appetite for life.
etymology: From Middle English appetit, from Old French apetit (French appétit), from Latin appetitus, from appetere (“to strive after, long for”); ad + petere (“to seek”). See petition, and compare with appetence.

definition: Mint with apple-scented stems of southern and western Europe; naturalized in United States.
Nutlike seed of a South American palm; the hard white shell takes a high polish and is used for e.g. buttons.
Pie (with a top crust) containing sliced apples and sugar.
Any tree of the genus Malus especially those bearing firm rounded edible fruits.
etymology: From Middle English appeltre, appiltre, appultre, from Old English æppeltrēow, corresponding to apple + tree. Cognate with Danish æbletræ, Swedish äppelträd, Norwegian epletre, Icelandic eplatré.

definition: The practical application of anatomical knowledge to diagnosis and treatment.
The branches of mathematics that are involved in the study of the physical or biological or sociological world.
The discipline dealing with the art or science of applying scientific knowledge to practical problems.
A person who uses scientific knowledge to solve practical problems.
Subject to appointment.
example: In the United States, the Secretary of State is an appointed position.

definition: The act of putting a person into a non-elective position.
example: The appointment had to be approved by the whole committee.
etymology: From Middle English appoyntement, apoyntement, from Old French appointement, equivalent to appoint + -ment.

definition: A book containing a calendar and space to keep a record of appointments.
A book containing a calendar and space to keep a record of appointments.
The final path followed by an aircraft as it is landing.
The path that is prescribed for an airplane that is preparing to land at an airport.
Suitable for a particular person or place or condition etc.

example: The effectiveness of the drug was well established.
etymology: From effective + -ness.

definition: An electronic device that alters how a musical instrument or other audio source sounds.
example: Guitarists derive their signature sound or ‘tone’ from their choice of instrument, pickups, effects units, and guitar amp.

definition: Being effective without wasting time or effort or expense.
example: An efficient production manager.
etymology: 1398, “making,” from Old French, from Latin efficientem, nominative efficiēns, participle of efficere (“work out, accomplish”) (see effect). Meaning “productive, skilled” is from 1787.

definition: The production of eggs (especially in birds).
Urge on; cause to act.
example: The other children egged the boy on, but he did not want to throw the stone through the window.
etymology: * From Middle English eggen (“to incite; urge on; instigate”), from Old Norse eggja (“to incite”), from egg (“edge”). More at edge. * A variant of the archaic "edge on."

definition: The white part of an egg; the nutritive and protective gelatinous substance surrounding the yolk consisting mainly of albumin dissolved in water.
example: She separated the whites from the yolks of several eggs.
etymology: Probably a remodelled form of Middle English whit of an egge (“white of an egg”).

definition: The productiveness of a hen or other egg-laying animal.
An inflated feeling of pride in your superiority to others.
example: The cousin of ego on the father's side.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ego (“I”). Chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Ich as a noun for this concept from the pronoun ich (“I”). Doublet of I and Ich.

definition: (psychoanalysis) the part of the ego that contains an ideal of personal excellence toward which a person strives.
An act undertaken to increase your own power and influence or to draw attention to your own importance.
etymology: Originally US drug subcultures, late 1960s.

definition: Having eight units or components.
Having eight sides.
One of four playing cards in a deck with eight pips on the face.
Being one more than seventeen.
etymology: From Middle English eightetene, eiȝtene, ehtetene, from Old English eahtatīene, eahtatēne, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Cognate with West Frisian achttjin, Dutch achttien, German achtzehn, Danish atten.

definition: Add details, as to an account or idea; clarify the meaning of and discourse in a learned way, usually in writing.
example: She elaborated on the main ideas in her dissertation.
etymology: 1575, from Late Latin ēlabōrātus (“worked out”), past participle of ēlabōrō (“to work out”), from ē- (“out, forth, fully”) + labor (“work, toil, exertion”). More at e-, labour.

definition: Hinge joint between the forearm and upper arm and the corresponding joint in the forelimb of a quadruped.
example: The sides of windows, where the jamb makes an elbow with the window back.
etymology: From Middle English elbowe (“elbow”), from Old English elboga, elnboga (“elbow”), from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô (“elbow”), equivalent to ell + bow.

definition: Space for movement.
example: Hardly enough elbow room to turn around.

definition: A person who is older than you are.
example: We were presented to the village elder.
etymology: From Middle English eldre, from Old English eldra, yldra, ieldra, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô. The vowel change from a to e triggered by the following i is called umlaut or I-mutation.

definition: The card player on the dealer's left.
Selected as the best.
example: An elect circle of artists.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēlēctus, past participle of ēligō (“to pick out, choose, elect”), from ē- (“out”) + legō (“to pick out, pick, gather, collect, etc.”); see legend.

definition: Official who won the office in a free election.
A commission delegated to supervise an election.
The minimum share of the vote which a political party requires to secure any representation.
example: The Free Democratic Party got only 4.8% of the votes so did not meet the 5% election threshold and did not win any directly elected seats.
etymology: From election + threshold.

definition: The body of electors who formally elect the United States president and vice president.
Electrical conduction through a gas in an applied electric field.
A car that is powered by electricity.
A bill for money owed for electricity used.
A blanket containing and electric heating element that can be controlled to the desired temperature by a rheostat.
A car that is powered by electricity.
A device that delivers an electric current as the result of a chemical reaction.
The quantity of unbalanced electricity in a body (either positive or negative) and construed as an excess or deficiency of electrons.
A public utility that provides electricity.
A light insulated conductor for household use.
A flow of electricity through a conductor.
example: An electric current runs through this wire.

definition: Electrical conduction through a gas in an applied electric field.
A rotating power drill powered by an electric motor.
(physics) the potential energy of an electric charge in an electric field, or of an electric current in a magnetic field.
A transducer used to detect and measure light and other radiations.
A fan run by an electric motor.
A field of force surrounding a charged particle.
A small electric space heater.
An electrical discharge accompanied by ionization of surrounding atmosphere.
A hammer driven by electric motor.
An iron which uses resistive heating from an electric current.
A lamp powered by electricity.
Electric lamp consisting of a transparent or translucent glass housing containing a wire filament (usually tungsten) that emits light when heated by electricity.
A main that distributes electricity.
A meter for measuring the amount of electric power used.
(music) an electronic simulation of a pipe organ.
Receptacle providing a place in a wiring system where current can be taken to run electrical devices.
An oven that is powered by electricity.
A kitchen appliance for disposing of garbage.
The difference in electrical charge between two points in a circuit expressed in volts.
The product of voltage and current.
A kitchen range in which the heat for cooking is provided by electric power.
Any sluggish bottom-dwelling ray of the order Torpediniformes having a rounded body and electric organs on each side of the head capable of emitting strong electric discharges.
Relating to or concerned with electricity.
example: An electrical engineer.
etymology: From electric + -al.

definition: A discharge of electricity.
The therapeutic application of electricity to the body (as in the treatment of various forms of paralysis).
Receptacle providing a place in a wiring system where current can be taken to run electrical devices.
A physical phenomenon involving electricity.
The craft of an electrician.
A physical phenomenon associated with stationary or moving electrons and protons.
A bicycle that is built with a motor, the bicycle can be powered by the motor or pedalling of the cyclist.
A machine for performing calculations automatically.
A machine-readable version of a standard dictionary; organized alphabetically.
An image represented as a two dimensional array of brightness values for pixels.
A musical instrument that generates sounds electronically.
A form of music consisting of sounds produced by oscillating electric currents either controlled from an instrument panel or keyboard or prerecorded on magnetic tape.
(electronics) a system of interconnected electronic components or circuits.
(music) an electronic simulation of a pipe organ.
A form of mind sports where the primary aspects of the sport are facilitated by video games.
Text that is in a form that computer can store or display on a computer screen.
Military action involving the use of electromagnetic energy to determine or exploit or reduce or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Refined and tasteful in appearance or behavior or style.
example: Elegant handwriting.
etymology: From Late Middle English elegaunt, from Middle French elegant, ultimately from Latin ēlegāns, collateral form of present participle of ēligere, from ex- (“out of, from”) + legō (“choose, select, appoint”).

definition: Huge (to 9 ft.) extinct flightless bird of Madagascar.
etymology: Apparently from Marco Polo's description of the legendary roc as being capable of seizing a small elephant.

definition: Any plant of the genus Alocasia having large showy basal leaves and boat-shaped spathe and reddish berries.
etymology: From its general resemblance in form.

definition: Either of two large northern Atlantic earless seals having snouts like trunks.
Small tree or shrub of the southwestern United States having a spicy odor and odd-pinnate leaves and small clusters of white flowers.
Raised above the ground.
example: An elevated platform.

definition: A railway that is powered by electricity and that runs on a track that is raised above the street level.
A railway that is powered by electricity and that runs on a track that is raised above the street level.
The event of something being raised upward.
example: An elevation of the temperature in the afternoon.
etymology: From Old French elevation, from Latin elevatio, equal to elevate + -ion.

definition: Lifting device consisting of a platform or cage that is raised and lowered mechanically in a vertical shaft in order to move people from one floor to another in a building.
etymology: From elevate + -or.

definition: A man employed to operate an elevator.
example: In England they call an elevator man a ‘liftman’.

definition: Where passengers ride up and down.
A girl employed to operate an elevator.
A man employed to operate an elevator.
example: In England they call an elevator man a ‘liftman’.

definition: An operator of an elevator.
(formerly in Britain) an examination taken by 11 and 12 year old students to select suitable candidates for grammar school.
The act of removing or getting rid of something.
example: Everton require at least 3 goals in the second leg to avoid elimination from the FA Cup.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēliminātiō, from eliminate + -ion.

definition: A chemical reaction in which a molecule decomposes to two different molecules.
A tournament in which losers are eliminated in successive rounds.
In or to another place.
example: He went elsewhere.
etymology: From Middle English elswher, from Old English elles hwǣr and elles hwerġen (“elsewhere”); corresponding with else + where.

definition: An identifier that a person uses as their identity to communicate on the email system.
A message sent over the internet via the email system.
Enclosed firmly in a surrounding mass.
example: Found pebbles embedded in the silt.
etymology: From embed + -ed.

definition: Come out into view, as from concealment.
example: Suddenly, the proprietor emerged from his office.
etymology: First attested in the late 16th century. Borrowed from Middle French emerger, from Latin ēmergō (“to rise up or out”), from ē- (a variant of ex- (“out, forth”)) + mergō (“to dip, to sink”)

definition: A brake operated by hand; usually operates by mechanical linkage.
The branch of medicine concerned with the prompt diagnosis and treatment of injuries or trauma or sudden illness.
A room in a hospital or clinic staffed and equipped to provide emergency care to persons requiring immediate medical treatment.
Determined or actuated by emotion rather than reason.
example: It was an emotional judgment.
etymology: From emotion + -al.

definition: A person subject to strong states of emotion.
In an emotional manner.
example: At the funeral he spoke emotionally.
etymology: From emotional + -ly.

definition: Put into service; make work or employ for a particular purpose or for its inherent or natural purpose.
example: Our company employs hundreds of people.
etymology: Borrowed from French emploi (“job, employment”), the deverbal from employer (“to put to use, to employ”), first attested in the late 17th century.

definition: Having your services engaged for; or having a job especially one that pays wages or a salary.
example: Most of our graduates are employed.

definition: Contract between employer and employee.
An agency that finds people to fill particular jobs or finds jobs for unemployed people.
Loud and confused and empty talk.
A monument built to honor people whose remains are interred elsewhere or whose remains cannot be recovered.
Loud and confused and empty talk.
A dash that is one-half the length of an em dash.
etymology: Named for its width, which is equal to the width of the letter n or N, or approximately half the width of an em dash.

definition: Providing legal power or sanction.
example: An enabling resolution.

definition: A provision in a law that confers on appropriate officials the power to implement or enforce the law.
Legislation that gives appropriate officials the authority to implement or enforce the law.
Contribute to the progress or growth of.
example: I encouraged him during his race.
etymology: From Middle English encouragen, encoragen, from Anglo-Norman encoragier, from Old French encoragier. Displaced native Old English hiertan, tyhtan, and trymman. By surface analysis, en- + courage.

definition: The ultimate user for which something is intended.
The flattened end of a motor neuron that transmits neural impulses to a muscle.
A species whose numbers are so small that the species is at risk of extinction.
example: The federal government has added five more birds to the endangered species list.

definition: Put up with something or somebody unpleasant.
example: The new secretary had to endure a lot of unprofessional remarks.
etymology: From Middle English enduren, from Old French endurer, from Latin indūrō (“to make hard”). Displaced Old English drēogan, which survives dialectally as dree. Doublet of dure.

definition: A broad field of engineering dealing with energy efficiency, energy services, facility management, plant engineering, environmental compliance and alternative energy technologies.
Ensure observance of laws and rules.
example: The police are there to enforce the law.
etymology: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).

definition: The act of enforcing; ensuring observance of or obedience to.
etymology: From Old French enforcement, see enforce + -ment.

definition: A metal casting containing the cylinders and cooling ducts of an engine.
example: The engine had to be replaced because the block was cracked.

definition: The operator of a railway locomotive.
Engine does not run.
The discipline dealing with the art or science of applying scientific knowledge to practical problems.
example: He had trouble deciding which branch of engineering to study.

definition: Increase the level of.
example: This will enhance your enjoyment.

definition: Increased or intensified in value or beauty or quality.
example: Her enhanced beauty was the result of a good night's sleep rather than makeup.
etymology: From enhance + -ed.

definition: Affording satisfaction or pleasure.
example: The company was enjoyable.
etymology: From enjoy + -able.

definition: The pleasure felt when having a good time.
example: Few activities better the enjoyment of a hearty meal eaten in good company.
etymology: From enjoy + -ment.

definition: The act of enrolling.
etymology: From Middle French enrollement. See enroll + -ment.

definition: Take possession of.
example: She entered upon the estate of her rich relatives.

definition: Provide entertainment for.
example: To entertain friends with lively conversation.
etymology: From Middle English entertenen, from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir, from entre (“among”) + tenir (“to hold”), from Latin inter + teneō (“hold, keep”). For the noun, compare French entretien.

definition: An activity that is diverting and that holds the attention.
etymology: From Middle English entretenement (“support, maintenance”), from Old French entretenement; see entertain. Morphologically entertain + -ment.

definition: A wall unit containing sound and television systems.
Those involved in providing entertainment: radio and television and films and theater.
A feeling of excitement.
example: Try to curb your enthusiasm.
etymology: First attested from 1603, from Middle French enthousiasme, from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”) + οὐσία (ousía, “essence”).

definition: Having or showing great excitement and interest.
example: Enthusiastic crowds filled the streets.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιαστικός (enthousiastikós), from either ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós) or ἐνθουσιάζω (enthousiázō) + -τικός (-tikós).

definition: Examination to determine a candidate's preparation for a course of studies.
Examination to determine a candidate's preparation for a course of studies.
Someone who organizes a business venture and assumes the risk for it.
etymology: Borrowed from French entrepreneur (“one who undertakes or manages”), from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.

definition: The form of a word that heads a lexical entry and is alphabetized in a dictionary.
A flat (usually rectangular) container for a letter, thin package, etc.
example: Push the envelope.
etymology: PIE word *h₁én From French enveloppe. The engineering sense is derived from flight envelope. The verb is from the noun.

definition: The branch of biology concerned with the relations between organisms and their environment.
A feeling of grudging admiration and desire to have something that is possessed by another.
example: C. 1631-1636, John Ford, The Fancies Chaste and Noble Such as cleanliness and decency Prompt to a virtuous envy.
etymology: Displaced native Old English æfest and nīþ.

definition: A long narrative poem telling of a hero's deeds.
Poetry celebrating the deeds of some hero.
A sign indicating that the quantities on either side are equal.
Having the requisite qualities for.
example: Equal to the task.

definition: A cessation of normal operation.
A person or thing equal to another in value or measure or force or effect or significance etc.
example: Send two dollars or the equivalent in stamps.
etymology: From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”). By surface analysis, equi- + -valent.

definition: Two words that can be interchanged in a context are said to be synonymous relative to that context.
Capable of making an error.
example: All men are error-prone.

definition: A valve in a container in which pressure can build up (as a steam boiler); it opens automatically when the pressure reaches a dangerous level.
Get rid of.
A valve in a container in which pressure can build up (as a steam boiler); it opens automatically when the pressure reaches a dangerous level.
The minimum velocity needed to escape a gravitational field.
Someone who escorts and protects a prominent person.
etymology: Borrowed from French escorte, itself borrowed from Italian scorta.

definition: The choicest or most essential or most vital part of some idea or experience.
example: Essence of Jojoba.

definition: Absolutely necessary; vitally necessary.
example: Essential tools and materials.
etymology: From Late Latin essentiālis, from Latin essentia (“being, essence”).

definition: A prerequisite.
An oil having the odor or flavor of the plant from which it comes; used in perfume and flavorings.
etymology: Containing the essence of the plant's fragrance.

definition: In essence; at bottom or by one's (or its) very nature.
example: The argument was essentially a technical one.
etymology: From essential + -ly.

definition: Set up or found.
example: To establish a fact.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English establissen, from Old French establiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of establir (modern French établir), from Latin stabiliō, stabilīre, from stabilis (“firm, steady, stable”).

definition: The act of forming or establishing something.
example: It was the establishment of his reputation.

definition: A person who is authorized to act as an agent for the sale of land.
example: In England they call a real estate agent a ‘land agent’.

definition: A tax on the estate of the deceased person.
The condition of being honored (esteemed or respected or well regarded).
example: It is held in esteem.
etymology: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō. See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.

definition: Income tax paid periodically on income that is not subject to withholding taxes; based on the taxpayer's predicted tax liability.
And others (‘et al.’ is used as an abbreviation of ‘et alii’ (masculine plural) or ‘et aliae’ (feminine plural) or ‘et alia’ (neuter plural) when referring to a number of people).
example: The data reported by Smith et al.

definition: Time without end.
example: It's been an eternity since we last saw each other.
etymology: From Middle English eternyte, from Old French eternité, from Latin aeternitās. Displaced native Old English ēcnes.

definition: Of or relating to the philosophical study of ethics.
example: Ethical codes.
etymology: From ethic + -al, from Late Latin ethicus (“moral, ethical”), from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

definition: A system of principles governing morality and acceptable conduct.
A drug that is available only with written instructions from a doctor or dentist to a pharmacist.
A committee appointed to consider ethical issues.
A group that has different national or cultural traditions from the majority of the population.
Evaluate or estimate the nature, quality, ability, extent, or significance of.
example: It will take several years to evaluate the material gathered in the survey.
etymology: Back-formation from evaluation.

definition: A handbag used with evening wear.
Attire to wear on formal occasions in the evening.
Attire to wear on formal occasions in the evening.
example: I felt uncomfortably conspicuous, since I was the only man in evening dress.

definition: A man's white shirt (with a starch front) for evening wear (usually with a tuxedo).
A planet (usually Venus) seen at sunset in the western sky.
etymology: From evening + star. Cf. Old English ǣfensteorra.

definition: Small California annual with white flowers.
In every way; completely.
example: He was every inch a statesman.

definition: In three month intervals.
To or in any or all places; pronoun, location; quantifier: universal.
example: You find fast food stores everywhere.
etymology: From Middle English eauerihwer, from Old English æfre + gehwær. By surface analysis, every + where.

definition: Clearly revealed to the mind or the senses or judgment.
example: Evident hostility.

definition: A look that is believed to have the power of inflicting harm.
example: An amulet to protect children from the evil eye.
etymology: From Middle English ivel eie (“evil eye; envy”), from Old English eage yfel, a calque of Latin oculus malus, from oculus (“eye”) + malus (“bad, evil, wicked; destructive, hurtful, injurious; unfavourable, unlucky”).

definition: A spirit tending to cause harm.
Having an evil appearance.
Having evil thoughts or intentions.
Of or relating to or produced by evolution.
example: Evolutionary biology.

definition: Work out.
example: Over several years the author evolved the story originally drafted as a novella into a real epic.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē- (“out of”) (short form of ex) + volvō (“roll”).

definition: (of telephone numbers) not listed in the telephone directory.
example: An ex-directory number.
etymology: From ex- (“outside”) + directory.

definition: A man who was formerly a certain woman's husband.
etymology: From ex- + husband.

definition: A person who was formerly a spouse.
Be greater in scope or size than some standard.
example: Their loyalty exceeds their national bonds.

definition: The quality of excelling; possessing good qualities in high degree.
example: John Davies was awarded for excellence in the field of computer security.
etymology: From Middle English excellence, from Old French excellence, from Latin excellentia.

definition: Far beyond what is usual in magnitude or degree.
example: An exceptional memory.
etymology: From exception + -al.

definition: The charge for exchanging currency of one country for currency of another.
Not divided or shared with others.
example: They have exclusive use of the machine.
etymology: From Latin exclūsīvus, from excludere (“to shut out, exclude”), from ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudere (“to close, shut”).

definition: A right reserved exclusively by a particular person or group (especially a hereditary or official right).
example: The company was granted the exclusive right to exploit the oil resources of the province.

definition: The branch of the United States government that is responsible for carrying out the laws.
A person responsible for the administration of a business.
The officer second in command.
A secretary having administrative duties and responsibilities.
A session (usually of a legislative body) that is closed to the public.
Several exercises intended to be done in series.
System consisting of the parts of an engine through which burned gases or steam are discharged.
Drained of energy or effectiveness; extremely tired; completely exhausted.
example: The day's shopping left her exhausted.
etymology: From exhaust + -ed.

definition: A person who is voluntarily absent from home or country.
example: He lived in exile.
etymology: From Middle English exil, borrowed from Old French essil, exil, from Latin exsilium, exilium (“state of exile”), derived from exsul, exul (“exiled person”).

definition: The state or fact of existing.
example: Laws in existence for centuries.

definition: A poll of voters as they leave the voting place; usually taken by news media in order to predict the outcome of an election.
Being or from or characteristic of another place or part of the world.
example: Exotic plants in a greenhouse.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”).

definition: The act of increasing (something) in size or volume or quantity or scope.
example: The expansion of metals and plastics in response to heat is well understood.
etymology: Borrowed from French expansion, from Latin expānsiō. By surface analysis, expand + -sion.

definition: A bit with a cutting blade that can be adjusted to different sizes.
A bolt that has an attachment that expands as the bolt is driven into a surface.
(computer) a socket in a microcomputer that will accept a plug-in circuit board.
Belief about (or mental picture of) the future.
example: He struggled with his parents' expectations.
etymology: From Middle French expectation, from Latin exspectātiō, from exspectō (“expect”). By surface analysis, expect + -ation. Displaced native Old English wēn.

definition: A military campaign designed to achieve a specific objective in a foreign country.
example: A naval expedition.
etymology: From Middle French expédition, and its source, Latin expeditio.

definition: High in price or charging high prices.
example: Expensive clothes.
etymology: From Latin *expēnsīvus, from expendō (“to weigh out (money), to pay out”) (whence English expend). By surface analysis, expense + -ive. In the sense of "high-priced" has largely displaced dear.

definition: Having experience; having knowledge or skill from observation or participation.
etymology: From experience + -ed.

definition: The specific techniques used in conducting a particular experiment.
(statistics) a variable whose values are independent of changes in the values of other variables.
Skillfulness by virtue of possessing special knowledge.
etymology: Borrowed from French expertise. Compare gourmandise.

definition: Having come to an end or become void after passage of a period of time.
example: An expired passport.

definition: A statement that makes something comprehensible by describing the relevant structure or operation or circumstances etc.
example: The explanation was very simple.
etymology: From Latin explanatio (“an explanation, interpretation”), from explanare (“explain”); see explain. Morphologically explain + -ation. Displaced native Old English racu.

definition: Precisely and clearly expressed or readily observable; leaving nothing to implication.
example: Explicit instructions.
etymology: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

definition: A definition that gives an exact equivalent of the term defined.
In an explicit manner.
example: In his foreword Professor Clark puts it explicitly.
etymology: From explicit + -ly.

definition: Use or manipulate to one's advantage.
example: He exploited the new taxation system.
etymology: From Old French esploit (noun), esploitier (verb).

definition: The act of making some area of land or water more profitable or productive or useful.
example: The exploitation of copper deposits.
etymology: Borrowed from French exploitation, from exploiter (“exploit”), from Latin explicō (“unfold, deploy”). By surface analysis, exploit + -ation.

definition: Serving to explode or characterized by explosion or sudden outburst.
example: An explosive device.
etymology: From Latin explōs-, stem of the perfect passive participle of explōdō + the suffix -ive.

definition: A quantity of explosive to be set off at one time.
Device that bursts with sudden violence from internal energy.
Any unit for measuring the force of explosions.
Expose or make accessible to some action or influence.
example: Expose your students to art.
etymology: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”).

definition: A measurement of radiation in relation to its ability to produce ionization.
Photographic equipment that measures the intensity of light.
Give verbal or other expression to one's feelings.
Mail that is distributed by a rapid and efficient system.
A trust created by the free and deliberate act of the parties involved (usually on the basis of written documentation).
Send by express mail or courier.
example: Express-mail the documents immediately.

definition: Communicated in words.
A military formation for skirmishing; as widely separated as the tactical situation permits.
A mutually agreed delay in the date set for the completion of a job or payment of a debt.
example: They applied for an extension of the loan.
etymology: From Middle English extensioun, from Old French estension, from Latin extensiō, extensiōnem.

definition: An electric cord used to extend the length of a power cord.
A course offered as part of an extension service.
A ladder whose length can be extended.
An additional telephone set that is connected to the same telephone line.
An educational opportunity provided by colleges and universities to people who are not enrolled as regular students.
Large in spatial extent or range or scope or quantity.
example: An extensive Roman settlement in northwest England.
etymology: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin extensīvus, from Latin extensus.

definition: In a widespread way.
example: Oxidation ponds are extensively used for sewage treatment in the Midwest.
etymology: From extensive + -ly.

definition: The region that is outside of something.
example: The sticker was attached to the exterior of the package.
etymology: From Latin exterior.

definition: A doorway that allows entrance to or exit from a building.
A drive with its own power supply and fan mounted outside the computer system enclosure and connected to the computer by a cable.
An organ that is situated on or near the surface of the body.
Overtime play until one team is ahead at the end of an inning; e.g. baseball.
example: And we go to extra innings.

definition: Remove, usually with some force or effort; also used in an abstract sense.
example: Extract a bad tooth.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extractum, neuter perfect passive participle of extrahō, from ex- (“out of”) + trahō (“to drag”).

definition: The process of obtaining something from a mixture or compound by chemical or physical or mechanical means.
etymology: From Old French estraction, from Medieval Latin extractio.

definition: The point located farthest from the middle of something.
